title: Show r/algotrading: six strategy bots, an AI research loop with a critic, hard risk rules, all visible live
author: haxiboy
selftext:
**CryptoArena: six bots, one arena, real Binance data, fake money (for now)**

https://i.redd.it/8fzxpme77fwh1.png

  
I’ve been building a strategy lab where six bots with different styles trade simulated money on live Binance data, and everything they do is visible on a public dashboard: [https://arena.haxiboy.com](https://arena.haxiboy.com)

**The bots**  
A trend rider, a mean reverter, a breakout hunter, a 30-day swing trader, an experimental one and a cross-pair hunter. Each starts with the same virtual capital, trades one pair at a time (30-minute candles, \~30 liquid coins), and the same fees and slippage are charged to everyone.

**The research loop (the part I find most interesting)**  
AI agents propose new strategy ideas. A second model from a different family reviews each idea critically before anything runs. Surviving ideas go through back-test gates (net profit per trade after fees, drawdown, walk-forward, market regimes, untouched data), then run live on paper for 3 days against the current champion. Only a better strategy replaces it. The page shows the live decision feed, including the rejected ideas and why they failed. Most of them fail, which is the point.

**Risk rules no AI can change**  
Stop on every trade, daily loss limit, kill-drawdown, no leverage, position size from a risk budget. Bots start with tight limits and earn looser ones only by proven results (and lose them after a drawdown).

**The arena**  
Seasons end, the weakest bot is eliminated and restarts as a new generation.

**What you can see live:** price charts with entry/stop/trail/target levels and order markers, the order tape, equity vs Bitcoin buy-and-hold, the bots’ desk chatter, which AI helper did what and when, and the risk tiers.

**Under active development**  
This is a work in progress and I’m shipping changes almost daily: new strategy types, better risk handling, dashboard features. Expect things to move, break or look different when you come back. The roadmap includes long/short simulation, more strategy families and a stricter season elimination bar.

**Honest status:** it’s day 2. Everything is paper money, results are tiny and statistically meaningless so far (the bots are slightly up, Bitcoin itself moved more). I’m not selling anything and this isn’t advice. The goal is to see over months whether any of these strategies keeps an edge after costs. If one does, I’ll consider a small live instance later, separately and with real limits. Since the system keeps changing, I’m also keeping the history of what changed when, so results can be read in context.

I’d love feedback, especially on: the validation gates (what am I missing?), how you’d test for regime dependence, and what you’d want to see on the dashboard to trust or distrust a paper-trading result.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: a critic from a different model family is a nice touch, but it only ever sees the idea, not the tuning. most overfit sneaks in after it signs off, when the backtest gets rerun with tweaked params until it looks good. how many reruns does a surviving idea usually take?

replies.author: haxiboy
replies.body:
Good point, partly. The critic does see the actual params, not just the idea, and nothing gets rerun with tweaks: each spec is hashed and tested once.

But tweaks do happen another way. When a bot has a champion, the generator tries neighbours of it (nudge a threshold or lookback), and each one counts as a new experiment. So it’s multiple testing, yeah. About 800 tried so far, 16 got through the gates.

What I have against it is pretty weak: the required margin grows with the number of experiments (log-scaled, crude, not a proper deflated Sharpe), a complexity penalty, walk-forward and a holdout that all ideas share so it leaks over time. The only thing that can’t be tuned is the live paper run vs the champion, and that’s only a few days per idea.

If you know a better way to budget the multiple testing I’m all ears. That’s the weakest part right now.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 800 tried and 16 through is the number I'd watch, that's 2% and a few of those will be luck. if the gate's bar doesn't rise with the trial count, neighbours of a champion mostly re-test the same noise. deflating the sharpe by the number of tries handles it, or hold the last few months out and only look once.

replies.author: haxiboy
replies.body:
Fair, that was the weak spot, so I changed it.

Two things now: the newest 30 days are a lockbox that none of the research gates can see, and an idea that clears everything else gets exactly one look at it. Each look raises the bar for the next one, since the lockbox is a shared resource. And the validation bar is now deflated by the number of effective trials, counted as distinct idea skeletons (same structure, different numbers) in the last 30 days, not raw experiments. There’s also a cap on how many tweaks of one skeleton can run.

In a first dry run on the real data, the couple of ideas that had cleared all the old gates both failed the lockbox, which is a small sample but the direction I wanted.

Caveats: with \~25 days of validation data the textbook deflated-Sharpe bar is out of reach for anything, so I run it at a quarter of the full strength and let the lockbox do the real work. And since my lockbox is the newest window, it rolls forward and old lockbox data eventually becomes research data. A fixed reserve would be stricter.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: counting skeletons instead of param sets is a good unit, otherwise a grid search passes for one idea. the lockbox holds as long as nobody peeks at it while debugging, which is how most of them leak in practice.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Showing the rejected ideas and having a second model from a different family review each one before anything runs is a good design. The weak spot I'd look at is the 3-day paper trial against the champion, since with that many ideas some will win by luck, so I'd use a longer window and count how many challengers were tried. For regime dependence, label regimes using only information known at the time and see whether a strategy holds up in each, not just on average. To trust a paper result, I'd want the trade count, fees and equity against Bitcoin buy-and-hold shown next to it. Cymetica's Agent Tournaments is one place to see agents compared head-to-head on the same market.
